reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: A functional defecatory disorder in which the pelvic floor and external anal sphincter fail to relax, or paradoxically contract, during attempted defecation, obstructing outlet
Presents with straining, incomplete evacuation, hard or infrequent stools, and often the need for manual manoeuvres
Diagnosis requires objective evidence of impaired evacuation: paradoxical or non-relaxing puborectalis on manometry or defecography, together with an abnormal balloon expulsion test
The balloon expulsion test is a simple, useful screen, as inability to expel a filled rectal balloon supports dyssynergia
Defecography shows failure of the anorectal angle to open and poor or absent evacuation of contrast
Biofeedback-based pelvic floor retraining is the first-line and most effective treatment, aiming to restore coordinated relaxation during straining
Should be distinguished from slow-transit constipation, though the two can coexist
reference.pathophysiology: Anismus (dyssynergic defecation) is an acquired disorder of defecatory coordination in which the puborectalis and external anal sphincter contract paradoxically or fail to relax during straining, so the anorectal angle does not open and rectal pressure cannot overcome outlet resistance. It is generally a learned or behavioural maladaptation rather than a structural lesion, often reinforced by painful defecation or excessive straining. Rectal propulsive force may also be inadequate. The result is functional outlet obstruction with incomplete evacuation.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructed defecation from rectocele or intussusception
Anal fissure causing pain-related sphincter spasm
additionalInvestigations: Anorectal manometry demonstrating paradoxical or non-relaxing puborectalis on straining
Balloon expulsion test as a functional screen for dyssynergia
Defecography (fluoroscopic or MR) showing non-relaxation of the anorectal angle and impaired evacuation
Colonic transit study to identify coexisting slow transit
Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy to exclude mucosal or obstructing pathology
Rectal sensory testing where hyposensitivity is suspected
redFlags: New-onset symptoms with bleeding, weight loss, or anaemia
Suspicion of Hirschsprung's disease in a young patient (absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex)
A palpable mass or obstructive features suggesting a stricture or neoplasm
Neurological signs suggesting a spinal or cauda equina lesion
reference.prognosis: Biofeedback pelvic floor retraining achieves symptomatic improvement in the majority of adequately selected and motivated patients; response is poorer when slow transit or structural disease coexists.
pitfalls: Diagnosing dyssynergia on a single test rather than corroborating findings
Treating with laxatives alone while ignoring the need for biofeedback
Attributing pain-related spasm from a fissure to primary dyssynergia
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
